extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, AI-for-math researchers, and ML practitioners interested in automated theorem proving
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and desiderata for measuring the usefulness, reliability, and autonomy of language-model-based systems applied to mathematical research (proof generation, formalization, benchmarks, and scaffolds). Useful for comparing models, designing benchmarks, and judging solution quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Proof autonomy and rigor standard
rubrics_metrics.description: We consider that an AI model has answered one of our questions if it can produce in an autonomous way a proof that conforms to the levels of rigor and scholarship prevailing in the mathematics literature. In particular, the AI should not rely on human input for any mathematical idea or content, or to help it isolate the core of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the project-level definition of a correct solution: autonomy (no human-originated ideas or steering) plus conformity to mathematical standards of rigor and scholarship. Anti-patterns include semi-autonomous runs where humans provide pivotal hints or steer the approach (e.g., telling the model to 'try using a BSS barrier type argument').

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark passability (FrontierMath pass@1 metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: FrontierMath measures performance on numerical-answer problems using pass@1 accuracy (e.g., best models ~40% on Tiers 1-3, ~32% on Tier 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass@1 is a straightforward machine-gradable metric for numeric-answer benchmarks; useful as an objective performance number but limited to problems with easily-graded answers and thus not directly comparable to proof-generation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: FrontierMath difficulty axes (Background, Precision, Creativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems on FrontierMath are rated on a scale of 1-5 along the axes of required Background, Precision, and Creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axes provide finer-grained evaluation than a single pass/fail score: required background measures prerequisite knowledge needed, precision measures the need for exact technical correctness, and creativity measures originality of ideas. Use these to interpret model strengths/weaknesses (e.g., models correlate negatively with required background).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization / mechanized verification (Lean formalization as gold standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalized proofs (e.g., correctly formalized in Lean) are considered the 'gold standard' for confidence in correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible formalized proof provides high-confidence verification but is labor-intensive; the scarcity of fully formalized model solutions is a signal of the gap between informal-success and mechanized-certainty. Example: Tom de Groot's manually-orchestrated Lean formalization was singled out as gold-standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy vs semi-autonomy (degree of human prompting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish fully autonomous model-generated solutions from those produced with human guidance, iterative prompts, or expert feedback; the former is required by First Proof's autonomy criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting prompts and whether pivotal ideas originated from humans is necessary. Semi-autonomous runs that incorporate human-derived heuristics or explicit hints should not be scored as autonomous; transcripts help adjudicate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-seeking and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Models must be truth-seeking: they should avoid producing incorrect mathematics and be amenable to verification; lack of truth-seeking leads to outputs that are difficult and costly to detect as wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include models producing subtle incorrect proofs or confidently incorrect formalizations. Short-term mitigations include AI-assisted reviewers or gating, but these are imperfect. Long-term solutions include improved autoformalization and model-internal verification capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect and avoid nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should reliably detect when they are producing nonsense; currently they often fail to do so and can claim false formalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should measure false-positive rates (claims of correctness that are wrong) and the model's propensity to admit inability. Recent models sometimes admit inability more often, which is a positive signal. Anti-pattern: models that never concede uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition and identifiability of main ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of writing: good solutions make main ideas, obstructions, and the roadmap identifiable; many model-produced solutions are poorly written and make correctness hard to check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare model writeups to human official solutions: does the exposition introduce useful objects/terminology and make the structure clear? Evaluate readability, presence of a high-level sketch, and whether auxiliary constructions are explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on prior literature / shallow generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Models often solve problems by recognizing and adapting close precedents in the literature rather than deep new reasoning; success that depends on finding prior work is valuable but qualitatively different from novel reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether solutions essentially reproduce or adapt existing arguments (e.g., problems 9 and 10 had answers available online). Benchmarking should distinguish retrieval/adaptation performance from genuine novel reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity and theory-building
rubrics_metrics.description: The capability to invent new definitions, techniques, or to 'theory-build'—produce genuinely new mathematical objects or frameworks—is a separate desideratum from solving posed problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure instances where models propose novel, useful definitions or techniques, and whether these lead to further fruitful developments. The essay notes little sign yet of autonomous large-scale theory-building, though seeds may exist in chain-of-thought traces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-horizon project reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to sustain tasks that take months or years of work (high-quality research projects) reliably—currently models are weak at long-horizon tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metrics like expected human-hours replaced, success probability over longer project timescales, and measures such as METR's estimate of hours-to-complete tasks at given reliability (e.g., GPT 5.2: 6.5 hours, 50% reliability for certain software tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and adaptation to novel objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Models' ability to 'learn' new mathematical objects, play with them, and develop expertise beyond static training corpora; currently limited, though scaffolds that leave notes to themselves can help slightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well a model can be introduced to a newly-defined object and then reason usefully about it without retraining. Consider measures of small-sample concept-uptake and internal note-taking effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and inference-scaling constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical evaluation must incorporate monetary/inference cost (e.g., GPT 5.2 Pro costs $168 per 1M tokens of output; per-query caps), since scaling inference or longer rollouts may be cost-prohibitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-solution expected token cost, compute time, and how performance scales with increasing inference budget. Consider 'capability at fixed cost' vs 'capability via increasing inference' as separate axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reproducibility (full transcripts and scaffolds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing full transcripts of model runs, scaffolding details, and reproducible scaffolds is essential for adjudicating autonomy and correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: DeepMind released transcripts for Aletheia which aided evaluation; lack of transcripts (OpenAI) complicates understanding how much human expertise contributed. Best practice: publish complete transcripts, prompts, scaffold orchestration, and environment details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark representativeness (measuring the right things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarks should measure abilities relevant to real mathematical research, and be careful about conflating model knowledge (vast corpora) with reasoning; current benchmarks may overstate model reasoning by rewarding retrieval/shallow generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design benchmarks to require genuine generalization, novel idea generation, or long chains of unassisted reasoning when appropriate. Interpret benchmark gains with attention to whether they reflect increased knowledge base or improved reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garbage generation rate / precision vs recall of useful outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the proportion of model outputs that are useful vs 'garbage' (nonsense or incorrect work); current scaffolds/models produce an enormous amount of garbage alongside some correct solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify signal-to-noise: number of credible partial solutions per many generated attempts, and overhead of filtering. High garbage rates increase human verification cost and reduce practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-valid-solution (human labor as automation barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical metric is the amount of human labor or hinting required to coax a correct proof from a model (e.g., one-sentence idea or many hours of back-and-forth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record median human-hours or hint-length to reach a correct solution; view this as the barrier to full automation (e.g., 8 hours of back-and-forth is actionable to automate through scaffolds).
